source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of exact tab-separated Greek payload, retaining whitespace and variant markers.

notes: The verb can refer to gathering or eating together. The shared-meal sense fits the embodied resurrection setting, while the command itself is clear.
The movement from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the earth’s end supplies a geographic program for Acts; ‘witnesses’ includes testimony that may become costly.
The women, Mary, and Jesus’ brothers are explicitly present in the praying community.
The Greek address is grammatically masculine but refers to the gathered community; ‘brothers and sisters’ communicates that inclusive audience.
The account graphically describes Judas’s body bursting open. The translation retains the harm without embellishment.
The replacement candidate in this episode is required to be a man who accompanied the group from John’s baptism through the ascension and can witness to the resurrection.
‘His own place’ is deliberately restrained. The verse does not name or describe Judas’s destination.
vocabulary: One who is sent, an apostle or authorized messenger.
Witness; later usage also gives English the word martyr.
Lot, allotted share, or assigned portion.

notes: The same word can mean tongue or language. The crowd hears recognizable native languages declaring God’s works.
The gathered diaspora worshipers are Jewish people from many nations. Pentecost begins within Israel’s story rather than replacing it.
Joel’s promise explicitly includes sons and daughters, young and old, and male and female slaves as Spirit-empowered speakers.
The verse holds God’s determined plan and foreknowledge together with the responsibility of those who handed Jesus over and killed him.
‘Pains of death’ uses the image of birth pains or binding cords. The main text retains the striking pain image.
Hades is the realm of the dead, not here a detailed description of final punishment.
The grammar closely joins repentance, baptism in Jesus’ name, forgiveness, and the Spirit’s gift without answering every later debate about their sequence.
The believers hold possessions in common and distribute according to need. The text describes concrete economic sharing, not only generous feelings.
vocabulary: Pentecost, the fiftieth day and Jewish Festival of Weeks.
Together with one purpose or common impulse.

notes: The man has been unable to walk since birth. Person-first wording preserves his humanity without hiding his lifelong condition.
The word for Jesus can mean servant or child. ‘Servant’ connects Jesus with the servant language of Scripture; the filial title is expressed elsewhere.
The crowd asks for a murderer to be released. The narrative names the lethal harm plainly.
‘Author’ can also mean leader, pioneer, or originator. The title creates a deliberate paradox: people kill the source or leader of life.
The relationships among Jesus’ name, faith in the name, and faith through Jesus are dense. The translation retains each phrase rather than assigning healing to human confidence alone.
Repentance and return lead into erased sins and seasons of refreshing; heaven receives Jesus until the promised restoration of all things.
The quotation’s ‘brothers’ means the people’s own kin. Refusal to hear the prophet brings severe exclusion from the people.
‘Offspring’ is singular in form and can be heard corporately or with messianic focus. The main text preserves the collective promise to all earth’s families.
vocabulary: Name, including identity, authority, and reputation.
Repent, change one’s mind and direction.

notes: The count specifies about five thousand men; it does not provide a total for women and children who may also have belonged to the community.
The verb can mean healed or saved. The man’s bodily restoration and the sermon’s saving claim deliberately share language.
The rejected stone becomes the head of the corner, either a cornerstone or capstone. ‘Cornerstone’ preserves the familiar building image.
Peter’s claim about salvation in Jesus’ name is translated directly without expanding it into a judgment about people or circumstances not under discussion.
‘Uneducated and ordinary’ describes the council’s social assessment: men without scribal training or official standing, not people lacking intelligence.
‘Sovereign Lord’ renders a title emphasizing ownership and authority; the prayer immediately names God as Creator.
The pinned text includes variant-marked language identifying the Holy Spirit as speaking through David’s mouth. The words are present and translated.
The prayer names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and Israel’s peoples as agents while also confessing God’s prior purpose. Neither agency is erased.
Unity of heart and soul takes material form: possessions are not treated as exclusively private, and distribution follows actual need.
vocabulary: Boldness, openness, or freedom of speech.

notes: Ananias and Sapphira retain control of the property and its proceeds; Peter identifies their sin as a coordinated lie about the gift. The deaths remain disturbing and are not softened into metaphor.
The growing community explicitly includes large numbers of both men and women.
People hope Peter’s shadow will fall on the sick. The narrative reports their action without stating that the shadow itself heals.
The word can mean zeal or jealousy. The leaders’ subsequent imprisonment of the apostles favors the hostile sense ‘jealousy.’
The officers avoid violence because they fear being stoned by the crowd. The threat of collective violence is explicit.
‘Tree’ is the ordinary word for wood and evokes scriptural language about a person hung on a tree.
‘Leader’ can also mean pioneer or originator. It is paired here with Savior.
Gamaliel refers to Theudas and Judas the Galilean as past examples. The translation preserves Luke’s sequence without attempting to solve external chronological questions inside the text.
The council has the apostles beaten and shamed. Their joy does not make the abuse good; it concerns being counted worthy for the Name.
vocabulary: The Name, a reverent way of referring to Jesus’ identity and authority.

notes: The Hellenists and Hebrews are Greek-speaking and Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking Jewish believers. The conflict concerns unequal daily care for their widows, not a division between Jewish and non-Jewish Christians.
Service at tables and service of the word use related ministry language. The apostles distinguish responsibilities without declaring material care unspiritual.
The selected seven are men in this narrated appointment. The wider address ‘brothers and sisters’ includes the whole community making the selection.
Nicolaus is identified as a convert to Judaism from Antioch, preserving both his adopted religious community and geographic origin.
‘Freedmen’ likely refers to formerly enslaved people and their descendants associated with the named synagogue.
The men are secretly induced, and the narrative calls the resulting witnesses false. Their accusations are reported as accusations, not accepted as fact.
Stephen’s face is compared to an angel’s face. The image describes what the council sees without removing the danger of the hearing.
vocabulary: A freed person or member of a freedmen’s community.
